title: Proposing one-sided tetrons as topological qubits for Majorana-based quantum computation
abstract: One-dimensional SM-SC hybrid nanowires with Rashba spin-orbit coupling and applied Zeeman field can support Majorana zero modes (MZMs) at the ends of the wire. In finite-length systems, residual wave-function overlap between the end modes produces an energy splitting. In a two-sided tetron qubit, composed of a pair of parallel Majorana wires coupled by a trivial SC backbone in the middle, this splitting limits the parity lifetime associated with Majorana pairs involving both wires and the coherence of the qubit, adversely affecting measurement-based braiding and readout operations. Here, we propose a one-sided tetron made of four parallel Majorana wires connected at a common end by an SC backbone. In the topological phase, the free wire ends host four MZMs that define the topological qubit, while the Majoranas localized near the opposite ends hybridize through the backbone and acquire finite energy. To study the basic hybridization mechanism, we consider a simpler two-wire subsystem, i.e., half of a one-sided tetron, which we call a doublon. In a doublon, the backbone, or bridge, strongly hybridizes the two Majorana modes at the connected end and shifts them away from zero energy, while the modes at the free ends form a near-zero energy fermion. We show that the splitting of the surviving MZM pair can fall by about two orders of magnitude compared to the splitting energies in a two-sided tetron, thereby dramatically increasing the parity lifetimes. Thus, the one-sided tetron ensures a suppression of the Majorana overlap comparable to doubling the length of the corresponding two-sided tetron.
summary: This paper proposes a novel 'one-sided tetron' architecture to improve Majorana-based topological qubits by mitigating detrimental wave-function overlap between end modes. By analyzing a simplified 'doublon' subsystem, the authors show that this geometry suppresses the energy splitting of the surviving Majorana pair by several orders of magnitude compared to existing designs. This enhancement dramatically increases the qubit's parity lifetime, moving closer to practical quantum computation.
main_problem: Residual wave-function overlap between end modes in finite-length Majorana systems limits the parity lifetime and coherence of qubits, hindering reliable quantum computation.
main_result: The proposed one-sided tetron geometry significantly suppresses Majorana overlap compared to two-sided tetrons, dramatically increasing the parity lifetime by orders of magnitude.
method: Theoretical modeling using effective low-energy Hamiltonians and analyzing hybridization mechanisms in simplified subsystems (doublons).
model_or_system: The system involves topological qubits realized using Majorana Zero Modes (MZMs) in semiconductor-superconductor (SM-SC) hybrid nanowires. The comparison is between two-sided and the proposed one-sided tetron structures.
key_observables: Parity lifetimes ($	au_X, 	au_Z$), Majorana splitting energy ($E_{ij}$), and the hybridization energy ($\delta$).
important_parameters: The degree of Majorana overlap, the size of the superconducting bridge, and the resulting energy splitting ($\delta$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the assumption that the one-sided tetron geometry can effectively decouple the end modes, mimicking the effect of doubling the wire length.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically compares the two-sided tetron and the proposed one-sided tetron, with a specific focus on the 'doublon' subsystem analysis.
paper_structure: The paper first identifies the limitation of two-sided tetrons due to overlap, then proposes the one-sided tetron. It analyzes the basic hybridization mechanism using a doublon model, demonstrating the dramatic improvement in parity lifetime, and concludes by comparing the suppression efficiency to existing designs.
why_interesting: The work directly addresses the coherence and lifetime limitations of topological qubits, which is central to quantum information science. The mechanism of suppressing overlap through geometry is highly relevant for designing robust quantum hardware.
